podcast.title: Dissemination via Radio (WWII Era)
podcast.body: Jump Blues emerged as part of a new "melting pot" of sounds, which gained widespread dissemination through radio during World War II. The challenges faced by Big Bands and the American Federation of Musicians strike created an opportunity for genres like Jump Blues to be heard by a wider audience for the first time. "Boogie-Wooogie, Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, Spear Trolls, a whole new melting pot of sounds was created and disseminated through the radio as a result of the big band problems and the musician's strike."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Jump blues is one of the primary Black Music genres from which rock and roll, and subsequently alt rock, substantially descended. "It's only right, given that rock and roll is descended substantially from Black Music, the blues, rhythm and blues, jump blues, jazz, gospel, and so many other genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Jackson's 1940s Homage
podcast.body: Joe Jackson's 1981 album "Jumpin' Jive" was entirely devoted to the sounds of 1940s Jump Blues and Big Band Jazz. This album, which included a minor UK hit cover of Cab Calloway's "Jumpin' Jive," highlighted Jackson's eclectic tastes and successful artistic experimentation. "And he devoted his fourth album, 1981's Jump and Drive, to the sound of 40's Big Band Jazz and Jump Blues."

podcast.title: The Kansas City 5's Primary Style
podcast.body: The Kansas City 5, an early incarnation of The Animals, predominantly played jump blues, a musical area where the tastes of Eric Burden and John Steele converged, covering artists like Ray Charles, Louis Jordan, and Big Joe Turner. "The Kansas City group played mostly jump blues, which was the area of music where burden and steel's tastes intersected."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
